2: Why does cloud D N S need a deck of its own?
Book 08 of the workbook asks for one authoritative policy and state plane that every other D N S system consumes.
Cloud D N S services are synchronized targets or forwarding destinations, not independently authored sources.
The warning is about authoring copies in every silo.
That produces split-brain answers, names that work in one cloud but not another, and uneven Protective D N S and logging.
The workbook already covers Infoblox with Azure and AWS.
It covered the Route 53 Resolver thinly, and Oracle Cloud only at the comparison level, so Part 1 adds both in depth.
BIND in a cloud wasn't covered at all; that's Part 2.
3: Here is the answer in brief.
Use the native resolver as the forwarding bridge in each cloud, and keep the policy in the D D I plane.
The Route 53 VPC Resolver and the Azure D N S Private Resolver are managed, zone-redundant forwarding services, and both providers recommend them over D N S servers on virtual machines.
Oracle Cloud gives every virtual cloud network, or VCN, a dedicated resolver that does the same job.
None of the three is an authority for the agency's own namespaces, and neither AWS nor Azure signs private zones.
Oracle Cloud is the one with no native D N S-layer filter for private D N S, so in a VCN the agency's policy applies only if queries are forwarded to agency resolvers.
And, as design guidance, run your own D N S servers in a cloud only for a stated reason.
4: AWS renamed the Route 53 Resolver the Route 53 VPC Resolver when it introduced Route 53 Global Resolver.
Several AWS pages still use the older name, so both appear in runbooks.
Every VPC reaches it at the VPC's base address plus two, called VPC plus two.
It answers the VPC's own EC2 names and records in private hosted zones associated with the VPC, and it recurses for public names.
Each network interface may send 1,024 packets per second to link-local services, shared by D N S and other services.
It can't be raised, and traffic over it is rejected.
That matters to any D N S server on EC2 that forwards to VPC plus two.
Route 53 Global Resolver is a different thing, an internet-reachable resolver for branches and on-premises sites, listed in 30 commercial Regions and not in GovCloud.
5: Hybrid resolution in AWS runs through two kinds of endpoint.
An inbound endpoint lets outside resolvers forward queries into a VPC and get the answers it sees, private zones included.
It has at least two addresses, in different Availability Zones.
Each address handles up to 10,000 UDP queries per second, but as few as 1,500 under connection tracking.
It speaks plain D N S, D N S over HTTPS, and a FIPS 140-2 version of D N S over HTTPS, inbound only.
A second type, the delegation inbound endpoint, answers NS delegations.
An outbound endpoint goes the other way: it sends queries that match a forwarding rule from the VPC to the agency's resolvers.
It speaks only plain D N S and D N S over HTTPS, so there's no FIPS option outbound.
And sharing a rule shares its outbound endpoint too.
6: A forwarding rule names one domain and its target addresses.
The most specific matching rule wins, and a rule overrides a private hosted zone of the same name.
A rule for the root, a single dot, forwards almost everything.
System rules carve a subdomain back out of a forwarding rule, so it resolves locally, and delegation rules handle delegated subdomains.
Rules are shared through AWS Resource Access Manager.
The receiving account associates them with its VPCs but can't change or delete them.
Profiles go further, bundling zones, rules, firewall rule groups and logging settings, one Profile per VPC.
Private hosted zones answer only inside associated VPCs, up to 300 per zone, and an empty match returns NXDOMAIN, with no fallback to public D N S.
7: D N S Firewall applies rule groups of allow, alert and block rules.
It uses custom or AWS managed domain lists, and the managed lists can't be browsed.
The Advanced tier detects domain generation algorithms and D N S tunneling.
It filters only queries that pass through the VPC Resolver, including those arriving through inbound endpoints, and by default it fails closed, with SERVFAIL.
Query logging records queries from the VPC, through the endpoints, and firewall actions, to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose.
It logs only queries that reach the VPC Resolver, and not answers from its cache.
DNSSEC: the VPC Resolver can validate public signed names, enabled per VPC.
Route 53 signs public hosted zones only.
And the VPC Resolver returns no DNSSEC records, so a resolver behind it can't validate for itself.
AWS warns that enabling validation could result in an outage.

That page doesn't mention the Resolver features, so the table draws on other AWS pages.
Resolver delegation is the conflict: the GovCloud guide says it's not available, and an April 2026 announcement says it is.
D N S Firewall and its managed lists: yes.
Of the Advanced protections, only dictionary DGA was announced for GovCloud; confirm the rest.
Signing of public zones: yes, with the key in U S-West.
Validation in the VPC Resolver isn't stated, so confirm.
9: Book 08's Chapter 07 covers the Private Resolver's hub-and-spoke design, so here is the summary with today's limits.
The inbound endpoint receives queries from on premises or other clouds and answers from private D N S zones linked to its virtual network.
There can be five per resolver, at 10,000 queries per second each.
The outbound endpoint and its forwarding ruleset send queries for named domains to target servers; a ruleset holds up to 1,000 rules, and a virtual network links only one ruleset.
It's a single-region service, zone-redundant inside the region, and it doesn't work in encrypted virtual networks or I P version six-enabled subnets.
And Azure D N S doesn't support zone transfers, so a BIND server can't be a secondary of an Azure private zone, or the reverse.
10: Azure's D N S-layer filter is D N S resolver policy.
Microsoft renamed it from D N S security policy, so expect both names.
A resolver policy filters and logs every query in a linked virtual network, public and private, with allow, block and alert rules.
It includes a Microsoft-managed threat intelligence list from the Microsoft Security Response Center.
Its logs go to Log Analytics, in the D N S query logs table, or to storage or Event Hubs, through diagnostic settings.
Microsoft lists resource logs only for resolver policies, so the inference is that per-query logs come from a resolver policy, or Azure Firewall's D N S proxy, not from the resolver itself.
DNSSEC: Azure can sign public zones, but the Azure-provided resolver doesn't validate.
No Microsoft page describes signing private zones, or whether the Private Resolver validates, so confirm that.
11: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure matters here because the H R platform runs on Oracle Cloud.
Every VCN gets a dedicated resolver, listening on 169.254.169.254.
It answers from the private views attached to it, in order, then its default view, then its resolver rules, then the internet.
Oracle says it performs recursion to the internet and DNSSEC validation for signed zones.
The trap is in that order.
A match in the sequence ends resolution, even an NXDOMAIN.
So a private zone for example dot com hides a forwarding rule for onprem dot example dot com. Views can be attached to many resolvers, sharing private D N S data across VCNs in a region.
Same-name private and public zones give split-horizon D N S.
Between VCNs, resolution uses resolver endpoints over a peering gateway.
12: A listening endpoint receives queries from on premises or other VCNs.
A forwarding endpoint sends queries no view answers to targets, under up to 50 resolver rules.
A rule matches a client address block, a domain, or None, which matches any query.
Forward is the only action, the first match wins, and an unreachable target ends processing.
A subnet's DHCP options can name a custom resolver of up to three D N S servers.
Those instances reach private views and rules only if 169.254.169.254 is in that list.
There's no native D N S-layer policy: no Oracle page describes a D N S firewall for the VCN resolver.
Private resolver logs, with each query's resolution path, are documented for the commercial realms only.
And the resolver can serve stale answers for up to 24 hours.

14: The U S Government Cloud is its own realm, called OC2, with U S Gov East in Ashburn and U S Gov West in Phoenix, and it holds a fed-ramp High authorization.
And its D N S A P I is for private D N S only; public D N S isn't available in the government realms.
The fed-ramp Marketplace lists the Government Cloud at High, and no commercial Oracle infrastructure offering.

15: How do the three meet on-premises D N S?
The same way, and Book 08's Decision 3 already holds the rules, as design guidance.
Into the cloud: on-premises resolvers, and other clouds' resolvers, conditionally forward each cloud namespace to that cloud's inbound endpoint, using static addresses written once.
On Oracle Cloud, the entry point is a listening endpoint.
Neither the AWS nor the Azure inbound endpoint accepts an ordinary NS delegation of a private zone; AWS's delegation inbound endpoint is the exception, and it's new.
Out of the cloud: each cloud forwards the agency's namespaces back to the agency resolvers, by its rules.
On AWS, create the rules once in a network account and share them through Resource Access Manager or a Profile.
Spokes associate them and can't edit them.
That's the cloud form of one policy object.
16: sis-uh requires Protective D N S for all egress D N S resolution, including from agency cloud deployments, directly or through agency D N S.
None of the native resolvers forwards the default path to Protective D N S on its own.
That takes a root rule in AWS or Azure, or a rule whose condition is None in Oracle Cloud, pointing at the agency resolvers.
Whether cloud egress already reaches it some other way is for the agency to confirm with sis-uh.
The clouds' own filters are a second policy surface beside the agency's response policy zones.
The design guidance: feed them from the same indicator decisions, or use them as a backstop, so a block on premises is also a block in each cloud.
Oracle has no such filter for private D N S, so its catch-all rule is the only way agency policy reaches a VCN.
Third, logs: all three go to the sim, parsed through ASIM's D N S schema, as Book 12 does.
17: To close Part 1, here's what the providers don't settle, so confirm it with them.
AWS: Resolver delegation and DNSSEC validation in GovCloud.
Azure: the Private Resolver's and resolver policy's availability in each Azure Government region, and whether the Private Resolver validates DNSSEC.
Oracle: private resolver logging in the government realm, and whether the VCN resolver passes DNSSEC data to a resolver behind it.
And sis-uh: whether Protective D N S returns DNSSEC data to agency forwarders.
